claim: Periodontitis affects 11.2% of the global population.
source: Periodontitis affects 11.2% of the global population and more than 40% of people over the age of 30, posing a major burden on public health (Eke et al., 2020; Sanz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eke et al., 2020 and Sanz et al., 2020

claim: Periodontitis affects more than 40% of people over the age of 30.
source: Periodontitis affects 11.2% of the global population and more than 40% of people over the age of 30, posing a major burden on public health (Eke et al., 2020; Sanz et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Eke et al., 2020 and Sanz et al., 2020

claim: The prevalence and severity of periodontitis increase with age.
source: Clinical studies have shown that the prevalence and severity of periodontitis increase with age, and moderate loss of alveolar bone and periodontal attachment is common in older adults (Huttner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huttner et al., 2009

claim: Moderate loss of alveolar bone and periodontal attachment is common in older adults.
source: Clinical studies have shown that the prevalence and severity of periodontitis increase with age, and moderate loss of alveolar bone and periodontal attachment is common in older adults (Huttner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Huttner et al., 2009

claim: Cell senescence is characterized by irreversible proliferation arrest, resistance to apoptosis, and secretion of inflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and proteases known as SASPs.
source: Cell senescence is a stress response characterized by irreversible proliferation arrest, resistance to apoptosis, and secretion of a range of inflammatory cytokines, growth factors, and proteases, known as senescence-associated secretory phenotypes (SASPs) (Coppé et al., 2010; Rodier et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coppé et al., 2010 and Rodier et al., 2009

claim: Cellular senescence is necessary for tissue homeostasis by eliminating unnecessary damage and promoting tissue repair through immune-mediated mechanisms.
source: Cellular senescence is considered necessary for tissue homeostasis as it aims to eliminate unnecessary damage and promote tissue repair through immune-mediated mechanisms and even prevent the occurrence of tumors (Campisi, 2013; Ohtani and Hara, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campisi, 2013 and Ohtani and Hara, 2013

claim: Cellular senescence can prevent the occurrence of tumors.
source: Cellular senescence is considered necessary for tissue homeostasis as it aims to eliminate unnecessary damage and promote tissue repair through immune-mediated mechanisms and even prevent the occurrence of tumors (Campisi, 2013; Ohtani and Hara, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Campisi, 2013 and Ohtani and Hara, 2013

claim: Persistent plaque in periodontal tissue results in oxidative DNA damage as collateral damage of chronic bacterial infection.
source: However, the specific environment of the gingival sulcus leads to persistent plaque in periodontal tissue, resulting in oxidative DNA damage as collateral damage of chronic bacterial infection (Aquino-Martinez et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aquino-Martinez et al., 2020

claim: Repeated exposure to lipopolysaccharide derived from Porphyromonas gingivalis can accelerate cellular senescence driven by DNA damage.
source: Repeated exposure to lipopolysaccharide (LPS) derived from Porphyromonas gingivalis (Pg), a key pathogen of periodontitis, can accelerate cellular senescence driven by DNA damage (Aquino-Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Aquino-Martinez et al., 2021

claim: Bacteria can induce senescence of healthy cells in an active oxygen-dependent manner by causing inflammation and excessive neutrophil activity.
source: Furthermore, recent evidence suggests that bacteria can also induce senescence of healthy cells in an active oxygen-dependent manner by causing inflammation and excessive neutrophil activity (Guo et al., 2024; Lagnado et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guo et al., 2024 and Lagnado et al., 2021

claim: Senescent cells contribute to bacteria-induced inflammation through the activation of SASPs.
source: Senescent cells have been found to contribute to bacteria-induced inflammation, with the activation of SASPs playing a crucial role in the release of various pro-inflammatory factors, including interleukin (IL)-1α, IL-6, and IL-8.
evidence: Statement about the role of senescent cells in inflammation

claim: Elevated levels of IL-1α, IL-6, and IL-8 have been associated with periodontal damage and loss of alveolar bone.
source: Elevated levels of these inflammatory factors have been associated with periodontal damage and loss of alveolar bone (Aquino-Martinez et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aquino-Martinez et al., 2020 and Yu et al., 2024

claim: Dendritic cells infected by Porphyromonas gingivalis activate SASPs such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, which accelerate the progression of periodontitis.
source: In the immune response to periodontitis, dendritic cells infected by Pg activate related SASPs, such as IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8, which ultimately accelerate the progression of periodontitis (El-Awady et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to El-Awady et al., 2022

claim: The aging of T lymphocytes leads to a significant alteration in their immunosuppressive ability in Th17/Treg subsets, resulting in the loss of tooth support and alveolar bone.
source: Additionally, the aging of T lymphocytes, which are crucial for adaptive immunity, leads to a significant alteration in their immunosuppressive ability in Th17/Treg subsets. This alteration ultimately results in the loss of tooth support and alveolar bone (González-Osuna et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to González-Osuna et al., 2022

claim: SA-β-gal was scarcely expressed in the gingiva of young healthy individuals.
source: In clinical gingival specimens from periodontally healthy individuals of similar age and those diagnosed with periodontitis, we found that the senescence biomarker senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) was scarcely expressed in the gingiva of young healthy individuals.
evidence: Based on experimental observation described in the text

claim: A notable increase in SA-β-gal-positive cells was observed in gingival samples from patients with periodontitis, primarily localized in the lamina propria of gingival connective tissue.
source: However, in gingival samples from patients with periodontitis, a notable increase in SA-β-gal-positive cells was observed, primarily localized in the lamina propria of gingival connective tissue (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Senescent biomarkers p16, p21, and H3K9me3 were significantly upregulated in human periodontitis gingival tissues.
source: Additionally, immunohistochemical (IHC) staining analysis revealed that other senescent biomarkers, such as cell cycle inhibitory proteins p16 and p21, and senescence-associated heterochromatin foci like H3K9me3, were significantly upregulated in human periodontitis gingival tissues as well (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The protein expression level of p16 in gingiva was significantly upregulated following ligation in the LIP mouse model, peaking at day 7 post-ligation.
source: IHC staining results indicated that the protein expression level of p16 among gingiva was significantly upregulated following ligation, peaking at day 7 post-ligation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 1D

claim: The protein levels of p16 in the LIP 7D group were about two times larger than those in the control group.
source: Western blotting analysis showed that the protein levels of p16 in the LIP 7D group were about two times larger than those in the control group (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The transcription of Cdkn2a, Cdkn1a, and Trp53 in gingival tissues was higher at day 7 post-ligation than those in control.
source: And the transcription of Cdkn2a (p16 encoding gene), Cdkn1a (p21 encoding gene), and Trp53 (p53 encoding gene) in gingival tissues was higher at day 7 post-ligation than those in control (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by qrt-PCR data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Bulk RNA sequencing identified 458 upregulated and 358 downregulated genes in LIP 7D compared to healthy mice.
source: Furthermore, bulk RNA sequencing was performed on gingival tissues from LIP 7D and healthy mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), identifying 458 upregulated and 358 downregulated genes.
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Among the upregulated genes in LIP 7D, 19 senescence-associated genes were detected, including C3 and Il-6.
source: Notably, among the upregulated genes, 19 senescence-associated genes were detected, including C3, Il-6, and so on (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by bulk RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: Several SASP genes including Icam1, Mmp3, Nos3, Igfbp7, Igfbp4, Mmp14, Timp1, Ngf, Il-6, Areg, and Vegfa were significantly upregulated in the LIP group.
source: We also observed a significant upregulation of several SASP genes such as Icam1, Mmp3, Nos3, Igfbp7, Igfbp4, Mmp14, Timp1, Ngf, Il-6, Areg, and Vegfa in the LIP group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: GSEA based on sequencing data revealed the upregulation of the cellular senescence pathway in LIP mice.
source: The gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) based on our sequencing data revealed the upregulation of the cellular senescence pathway in LIP mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: A significant reduction in oxidative phosphorylation and the tricarboxylic acid cycle was observed in the LIP group.
source: Moreover, a significant reduction in oxidative phosphorylation and the tricarboxylic acid cycle was observed in the LIP group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, C

claim: GO Biological Process analysis demonstrated mitochondrial respiratory and electron transport dysfunction, as well as impaired oxidative phosphorylation in the gingiva of LIP mice.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process analysis of differentially expressed genes further demonstrated mitochondrial respiratory and electron transport dysfunction, as well as impaired oxidative phosphorylation in the gingiva of LIP mice, suggesting that mitochondrial dysfunction might contribute to cell senescence in periodontitis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction might contribute to cell senescence in periodontitis.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) Biological Process analysis of differentially expressed genes further demonstrated mitochondrial respiratory and electron transport dysfunction, as well as impaired oxidative phosphorylation in the gingiva of LIP mice, suggesting that mitochondrial dysfunction might contribute to cell senescence in periodontitis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Inferred from GO analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: The cellular senescence pathway and inflammatory-related pathways including complement activation and response to lipopolysaccharide were enriched in the LIP group.
source: Meanwhile, upregulation of the cellular senescence pathway and a series of inflammatory-related pathways, including complement activation and response to lipopolysaccharide, were also enriched in the LIP group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D

claim: The PI3K–AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling pathways were activated in the LIP group.
source: Besides that, the PI3K–AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling pathways were also activated in the LIP group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), which were closely associated with the onset of cellular senescence and the secretion of SASP factors (Raynard et al., 2022; Sayegh et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F and citations

claim: The PI3K–AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling pathways are closely associated with the onset of cellular senescence and the secretion of SASP factors.
source: Besides that, the PI3K–AKT, MAPK, and NF-κB signaling pathways were also activated in the LIP group (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F), which were closely associated with the onset of cellular senescence and the secretion of SASP factors (Raynard et al., 2022; Sayegh et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Raynard et al., 2022; Sayegh et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023

claim: Senescent cells gradually accumulated during the progression of periodontitis.
source: Collectively, these findings suggested that senescent cells gradually accumulated and senescence-related signaling pathways were activated during the progression of periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: Senescence-related signaling pathways were activated during the progression of periodontitis.
source: Collectively, these findings suggested that senescent cells gradually accumulated and senescence-related signaling pathways were activated during the progression of periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: In periodontitis samples, immune cells increased while structural cells such as fibroblasts decreased.
source: In periodontitis samples, there was a notable shift in cellular composition: immune cells increased while structural cells, such as fibroblasts, decreased (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B, C

claim: Fibroblasts in periodontitis showed significant upregulation of senescence scores, indicating they had the highest overall levels of senescence.
source: Cellular senescence gene score analysis across different cell types revealed that fibroblasts in particular showed significant upregulation of senescence scores in periodontitis, indicating that they had the highest overall levels of senescence (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by cellular senescence score analysis shown in Figure 2D

claim: GSEA of differentially expressed genes between healthy and periodontitis fibroblasts confirmed the activation of senescence pathways in periodontitis.
source: GSEA of differentially expressed genes between healthy and periodontitis fibroblasts further confirmed the activation of senescence pathways in periodontitis (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Fibroblast proportion declined with increasing disease severity in periodontitis.
source: The results showed a decline in fibroblast proportion along with increasing disease severity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D) and a corresponding increase in cellular senescence score (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from GSE152042 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D and Figure 2F

claim: Cellular senescence score increased with increasing disease severity in periodontitis.
source: The results showed a decline in fibroblast proportion along with increasing disease severity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, D) and a corresponding increase in cellular senescence score (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data from GSE152042 shown in Figure 2F

claim: The proportion of p16+ senescent fibroblasts in periodontitis rose to approximately 25%, compared to very few in healthy gingiva.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) staining on clinical sample confirmed that the proportion of p16+ senescent fibroblasts in periodontitis rose to approximately 25%, compared to very few in healthy gingiva (Figure 2G).

claim: Healthy primary gingival fibroblasts stimulated with different concentrations of Pg-LPS showed a dose-dependent increase in SA-β-gal-positive fibroblasts.
source: In vitro, healthy primary gingival fibroblasts (HGFs) stimulated with different concentrations of Porphyromonas gingivalis lipopolysaccharide (Pg-LPS) showed a dose-dependent increase in SA-β-gal-positive fibroblasts (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: Gingival fibroblasts undergo significant senescence during the progression of periodontitis.
source: These findings suggest that gingival fibroblasts undergo significant senescence, potentially induced by Pg-LPS, during the progression of periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: Gingival fibroblast senescence is potentially induced by Pg-LPS.
source: These findings suggest that gingival fibroblasts undergo significant senescence, potentially induced by Pg-LPS, during the progression of periodontitis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations

claim: Subpopulations 1 and 3 of fibroblasts significantly increased in periodontitis compared to healthy controls.
source: The cell proportion bar chart revealed a significant increase in subpopulations 1 and 3 in periodontitis compared to healthy controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Fibroblast subpopulation 1 exhibited the highest average expression levels of cellular senescence genes, with a marked increase in periodontitis.
source: We then applied a cellular senescence gene set (Saul et al., 2022) to score these subpopulations and found that subpopulation 1 exhibited the highest average expression levels, with a marked increase in periodontitis (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by cellular senescence score analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: GO enrichment analysis confirmed that fibroblast subpopulation 1 displayed upregulated aging characteristics.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed genes further confirmed that subpopulation 1 displayed upregulated aging characteristics (Figure 3D), indicating that this subpopulation is primarily responsible for fibroblast senescence.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Fibroblast subpopulation 1 is primarily responsible for fibroblast senescence.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis of the differentially expressed genes further confirmed that subpopulation 1 displayed upregulated aging characteristics (Figure 3D), indicating that this subpopulation is primarily responsible for fibroblast senescence.
evidence: Inferred from GO analysis data shown in Figure 3D

claim: CD81 emerged as a potential biomarker for the senescent fibroblast subpopulation 1.
source: Among the top 20 marker genes for subpopulation 1, CD81, a transmembrane protein, emerged as a potential biomarker for this senescent subpopulation (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by marker gene analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: CD81 was predominantly enriched in fibroblast subpopulation 1.
source: A density heatmap demonstrated that CD81 was predominantly enriched in subpopulation 1 (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by density heatmap shown in Figure 3F

claim: The proportion of CD81+ fibroblasts in periodontitis increased to approximately 50%, compared to very few in healthy samples.
source: IF staining further showed that the proportion of CD81+ fibroblasts in periodontitis increased to approximately 50%, compared to very few in healthy samples (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by IF staining data shown in Figure 3G

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts might represent a core senescent fibroblast population in human periodontitis.
source: Thus, CD81+ fibroblasts might represent a core senescent fibroblast population in human periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited elevated levels of SASP-related genes, including IL-6, CXCL5, CXCL6, MMP1, and MMP3.
source: CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited elevated levels of SASP-related genes, including IL-6, CXCL5, CXCL6, MMP1, and MMP3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4A

claim: Pathways related to fatty acid biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, and steroid biosynthesis were significantly upregulated in CD81+ fibroblasts.
source: Pathways related to fatty acid biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, and steroid biosynthesis were significantly upregulated in CD81+ fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that lipid metabolism might play a role in cellular senescence of the gingival fibroblasts.
evidence: Supported by metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Lipid metabolism might play a role in cellular senescence of gingival fibroblasts.
source: Pathways related to fatty acid biosynthesis, arachidonic acid metabolism, and steroid biosynthesis were significantly upregulated in CD81+ fibroblasts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that lipid metabolism might play a role in cellular senescence of the gingival fibroblasts.
evidence: Inferred from metabolic pathway analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Arachidonic acid could be converted into prostaglandins and leukotrienes via cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases, contributing to the inflammatory response.
source: Arachidonic acid, in particular, could be converted into prostaglandins and leukotrienes via cyclooxygenases (COXs) and lipoxygenases, contributing to the inflammatory response (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021 and metabolic pathway diagram in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts showed higher gene expression of PTGS1 and PTGS2 compared to other fibroblast subpopulations.

evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts predominantly clustered at the end of the differentiation trajectory, indicating limited differentiation potential.
source: Pseudotime analysis of fibroblast differentiation trajectories revealed that CD81+ fibroblasts predominantly clustered at the end of the trajectory, indicating limited differentiation potential (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by pseudotime analysis shown in Figure 4B, C

claim: Functional enrichment analysis of genes showing gradual increases during differentiation highlighted pathways related to inflammatory activation and aging characteristics.
source: Functional enrichment analysis of genes showing gradual increases during differentiation highlighted pathways related to inflammatory activation and aging characteristics (Figure 4D).

claim: Several SASP genes including CXCL1, CXCL6, IL6, MMP1, SERPINE1, EGFR, FGF2, FNDC1, IGFBP4, LAMB1, and TIMP1 exhibited increased expression during fibroblast differentiation.
source: Several SASP genes, including CXCL1, CXCL6, IL6, MMP1, SERPINE1, EGFR, FGF2, FNDC1, IGFBP4, LAMB1, and TIMP1, also exhibited increased expression during differentiation (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis during differentiation shown in Figure 4E

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited differentiation arrest and heightened expression of SASP factors.
source: Overall, our bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited differentiation arrest and heightened expression of SASP factors, further implicating them in the inflammatory and senescent processes of periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple bioinformatics analyses

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts are implicated in the inflammatory and senescent processes of periodontitis.
source: Overall, our bioinformatics analysis demonstrated that CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited differentiation arrest and heightened expression of SASP factors, further implicating them in the inflammatory and senescent processes of periodontitis.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple bioinformatics analyses

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts had the highest level of communication with immune cells, particularly neutrophils, compared to other fibroblast subgroups.
source: Our results revealed that CD81+ fibroblasts had the highest level of communication with immune cells, particularly neutrophils, compared to other fibroblast subgroups (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by cell-cell communication analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts play a key role in mediating the immune response during periodontitis.
source: This suggests that CD81+ fibroblasts play a key role in mediating the immune response during periodontitis.
evidence: Inferred from cell-cell communication analysis

claim: A significant increase in the expression of MIF and C3 signaling pairs was observed between CD81+ fibroblasts and immune cells.
source: Additionally, we observed a significant increase in the expression of MIF and C3 signaling pairs between CD81+ fibroblasts and immune cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by cell-cell communication analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: C3 is known to recruit neutrophils and contribute to the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated the importance of sustained neutrophil infiltration in the progression of periodontitis, with C3 known to recruit neutrophils and contribute to the formation of neutrophil extracellular traps (Ando et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ando et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023

claim: The C3 receptor–ligand pair was active in the communication between CD81+ fibroblasts and neutrophils in both healthy and periodontitis conditions.
source: Further analysis of the C3 pathway showed that the C3 receptor–ligand pair was active in the communication between CD81+ fibroblasts and neutrophils in both healthy and periodontitis conditions (Figure 5C), underscoring its unique role in neutrophil recruitment.
evidence: Supported by C3 pathway analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited the highest expression of the C3 ligand compared to other fibroblast subgroups.
source: Notably, CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited the highest expression of the C3 ligand compared to other fibroblast subgroups, while the C3 receptor (C3aR1) was exclusively expressed by neutrophils in periodontitis (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: The C3 receptor (C3aR1) was exclusively expressed by neutrophils in periodontitis.
source: Notably, CD81+ fibroblasts exhibited the highest expression of the C3 ligand compared to other fibroblast subgroups, while the C3 receptor (C3aR1) was exclusively expressed by neutrophils in periodontitis (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Higher C3 expression was detected in human periodontitis gingiva.
source: We also detected higher C3 expression in human periodontitis gingiva (Figure 5E), indicating its involvement in the disease.
evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Periodontitis gingival fibroblasts secreted higher levels of C3 protein at 30 ng/ml compared to healthy fibroblasts at about 20 ng/ml.
source: In vitro experiments further confirmed that periodontitis gingival fibroblasts secreted higher levels of C3 protein at 30 ng/ml compared to healthy fibroblasts at about 20 ng/ml (Figure 5F), and Pg-LPS stimulation could enhance C3 secretion by gingival fibroblasts from baseline at 10 to about 20 ng/ml (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Pg-LPS stimulation could enhance C3 secretion by gingival fibroblasts from baseline at 10 to about 20 ng/ml.
source: In vitro experiments further confirmed that periodontitis gingival fibroblasts secreted higher levels of C3 protein at 30 ng/ml compared to healthy fibroblasts at about 20 ng/ml (Figure 5F), and Pg-LPS stimulation could enhance C3 secretion by gingival fibroblasts from baseline at 10 to about 20 ng/ml (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5G

claim: The regions expressing CD81 and SOD2 in periodontitis overlapped in the gingival lamina propria, showing a high spatial correlation.

evidence: Supported by spatial transcriptomic analysis shown in Figure 5H

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts might facilitate neutrophil infiltration through the C3/C3aR1 axis, contributing to the inflammatory response in periodontitis.
source: These findings suggest that CD81+ fibroblasts might facilitate neutrophil infiltration through the C3/C3aR1 axis, contributing to the inflammatory response in periodontitis.

claim: In the gingiva of the LIP model, p16+ fibroblasts comprised approximately 70% of total fibroblasts, significantly higher than the 10% observed in healthy mice.

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts accounted for about 30% of total fibroblasts in the LIP model, compared to less than 10% in the control group.
source: Similarly, CD81+ fibroblasts accounted for about 30% of total fibroblasts, compared to less than 10% in the control group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by IF staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: IF staining revealed co-localization of Vimentin, p16, and CD81 in LIP gingiva, indicating the presence of senescent CD81+ fibroblasts in the experimental periodontitis model.

claim: Higher expression of C3 protein was observed in the LIP group compared to controls.

claim: Neutrophil infiltration increased from approximately 10% at baseline to 40% in the inflamed gingiva of LIP mice.

claim: CD81+ C3+ fibroblasts constituted the majority of fibroblasts in the LIP group.

claim: MPO+ neutrophils clustered around CD81+ cells in the lamina of the LIP model.

claim: CD81+ fibroblasts with senescence characteristics might activate neutrophils through C3 in the LIP mouse model, similar to the mechanism observed in human periodontitis.

claim: The ABT263-treated group exhibited reduced inflammatory cell infiltration in the gingiva compared to the vehicle control.

claim: ABT263 administration resulted in a significant reduction in senescent cells: p16+ cells decreased from 20% to 8%, and H3K9me3+ cells from 35% to 20%.

claim: ABT263 treatment resulted in a drop in the proportion of CD81+ fibroblasts from 40% to less than 20%.

claim: IHC analysis revealed a slight reduction in C3 intensity in gingival tissue after ABT263 treatment.

claim: ABT263 treatment resulted in a significant decrease in the number of infiltrated neutrophils.

evidence: Supported by IHC staining data shown in Figure 6G, e

claim: A marked reduction in the number of osteoclasts marked by CTSK was observed in the ABT263-treated group, decreasing from 6 cells/mm² in the vehicle group to 1 cell/mm².

claim: Senolytic treatment with ABT263 could be a potential strategy to mitigate inflammation and bone resorption in periodontitis progression.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that senolytic treatment with ABT263 could be a potential strategy to mitigate inflammation and bone resorption in periodontitis progression.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations with ABT263 treatment

claim: Metformin has been preliminarily validated for its therapeutic efficacy in periodontitis.
source: Metformin, an oral antihyperglycemic drug, has been preliminarily validated its therapeutic efficacy in periodontitis (Neves et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neves et al., 2023

claim: Metformin regulates cellular senescence.
source: Increasing evidence suggests that metformin regulates cellular senescence, but its involvement in periodontitis-related senescence has yet to be reported (Kodali et al., 2021; Soukas et al., 2019).
